claims.text: Reducing interface thickness and introducing a compositional gradient in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers increases local interfacial misfit strain.
Increased interfacial misfit strain promotes preferential nucleation and accumulation of dislocations at FCC/BCC interfaces.
Preferential interfacial dislocation activity causes a transition to an interface-dominated creep regime under sustained loading.
The starting material is a nanoscale coating with alternating FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers and relatively thick, compositionally homogeneous interfaces.
Ni-based Cantor-alloy variants are examples of materials suitable for the proposed FCC/BCC multilayer.
Interface thickness and interfacial compositional gradient can be varied systematically as the controlled intervention.
The comparison should use sustained constant-stress loading at room temperature and 300–500 K.
In situ electron microscopy can be used to observe deformation-defect evolution during controlled mechanical loading.
Compositional grading and reduced interface thickness produce interfacial misfit-strain fields and dislocation networks.
High-entropy alloys possess compositional complexity and pronounced lattice distortion that affect dislocation behavior.
Compositional complexity and lattice distortion lower the energy barrier for dislocation nucleation specifically at regions of high interfacial misfit.
Dislocations nucleated at engineered interfaces accumulate and interact to form dense interfacial dislocation networks.
Dense interfacial dislocation networks control the creep deformation rate.
Thinner, compositionally graded interfaces will have higher local interfacial dislocation density than thicker, homogeneous interfaces.
Thinner, compositionally graded interfaces will produce enhanced strain gradients.
The proposed interface-mediated effect is expected to be most prominent at moderate stress and temperature.
At very high stresses or temperatures, increased dislocation mobility may mask the interface-mediated effect.

Failure to observe both a statistically significant increase in interfacial dislocation density and a transition to interface-dominated creep relative to thicker homogeneous interfaces would falsify the hypothesis.
